narrativeProgression.description: The scientist introduces the James Webb Space Telescope as the successor to the Hubble.
He highlights its increased size, power, and ability to measure longer infrared wavelengths.
He emphasizes the potential for new discoveries beyond Hubble's capabilities.
He outlines the telescope's goals: seeing further back in time, observing the formation of stars and planets, understanding galaxy growth, and potentially finding life-supporting planets.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The James Webb Space Telescope is the plan successor for the great Hubble Space Telescope.
It's much bigger, more powerful, and measures longer infrared wavelengths than what the Hubble can do.
And so that enables us to make discoveries that the Hubble cannot do.
And so we hope to see farther back towards the earliest parts of the universe.
We hope to see the formation of stars and planets nearby.
We hope to understand how the galaxies grow, what came even before the galaxies.
We even hope to find out whether planets around other stars could potentially support life.

youtube_description:
Dr. John Mather is a Nobel Laureate in Physics for his work on the Cosmic Background Explorer Satellite.  He is currently a Senior Astrophysicist at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center.

We sat down with Dr. John Mather to ask some questions about his career in science.  Mather told us about his trajectory from a childhood interest in science, through his education and into his career.  He also discussed the most interesting trends in science and provided advice for the scientists of tomorrow.

See more interviews with NASA scientists at http://www.saylor.org/scienceminded/
